h1: Moving from chef to brewer and the skills that carry over
title: Moving from Chef to Brewer | Craft Beer School
desc: Which kitchen skills transfer to brewing, which do not and what a chef needs to learn before applying for a brewer job in India.
teaser: Chefs already work hot, fast and clean. Brewing adds patience, chemistry and very large tanks.
standfirst: Chefs make good brewers more often than people expect. Palate, hygiene and working under pressure all carry across. The adjustment is in time scale, scale of kit and the discipline of recording everything.
sections: Your palate is the biggest asset

Professional cooks taste constantly. They can tell when a sauce needs acid or salt and they have a memory for flavour that most new brewers lack. In brewing that skill becomes sensory evaluation: tasting wort, green beer and finished beer and spotting faults early.

The vocabulary shifts. You will learn to name off-flavours such as diacetyl (butter), acetaldehyde (green apple) and dimethyl sulphide (cooked sweetcorn). Our guide to beer off-flavours lists the common ones. A chef who can pick these out quickly is useful from week one.

A good kitchen runs on cleaning as you go, separate boards for raw and cooked food and a strong sense of where contamination comes from. Brewing is the same, scaled up. Anything that touches cooled wort or beer must be clean and sanitised, because yeast is not the only microbe that likes sugar.

Brewery cleaning uses clean-in-place systems: hot caustic to remove soil, a rinse, acid to remove scale, a rinse and then a sanitiser. Caustic is often used at around 1 to 2% and well above 60 °C, so it needs gloves, goggles and respect. Chefs who already know HACCP from food safety training will find the brewery version familiar.
Mise en place becomes the brew sheet

Chefs prepare everything before service. Brewers prepare everything before mash in: malt weighed and milled, water treated, hops weighed by addition, yeast checked, vessels cleaned. A brew day goes wrong in the same way a service does, when something was not ready.

The difference is the record. A kitchen runs on memory and taste. A brewery runs on a brew sheet that logs every weight, temperature, time and gravity. That is not bureaucracy. It is how you make the same beer twice and how you find out what went wrong when a batch tastes off a month later.

A kitchen judges success in minutes. A brewery judges it in weeks. An ale might take two to three weeks from brew day to packaging. A lager can take five weeks or more because it ferments cool and matures cold. You will not know if today's decision was right until long after the shift.

That calls for patience and for trust in measurements. You cannot taste a lager at day two and fix it with a pinch of something. You check gravity, temperature and pH and let the yeast finish its work.

Kitchens are hard work. Breweries are hard in a different way: 25 kg malt bags, kegs that weigh around 60 kg when full, hoses, ladders and wet floors. Much of a junior brewer's day is cleaning and moving things. You also work around pressure vessels, hot liquids and carbon dioxide, which can build up in closed spaces.

Learn the safety basics early. Our guide on mechanical skills a brewer should pick up covers pumps, valves and gaskets, which a kitchen rarely prepares you for.
Where chefs often shine in brewpubs

Brewpubs in India sell food and beer side by side. A brewer who understands the kitchen can design beers that work with the menu, help with pairing and talk to guests about both. A crisp lager with a spicy Andhra dish, a wheat beer with a fragrant biryani or a malty amber with tandoori grills are the kind of matches a chef can explain with authority.

That makes you a strong candidate for brewpub roles in particular. It also helps that you already know restaurant hours and service pressure.
Fill the gaps before you apply

What most chefs lack is the science: how enzymes convert starch at mash temperatures of roughly 62 to 72 °C, how yeast behaves, what pH does and how to calculate alcohol from gravity. You also need numbers and spreadsheets, which our guide on spreadsheet skills for brewers covers.

Your first step: brew one batch at home or on a course and keep a full brew sheet as if a head brewer were going to read it. Bring that sheet to interviews along with your kitchen experience. It shows you already think like a brewer.
faqs: Can a chef become a brewer?
Yes. Palate, hygiene and working under pressure carry across well. Chefs need to add brewing science, record keeping and familiarity with brewery equipment.
What kitchen skill helps most in brewing?
Tasting. A trained palate helps with sensory evaluation and spotting off-flavours early, which is valuable from the first week.
Is brewing more physical than cooking?
Differently physical. Expect heavy malt bags and kegs, lots of cleaning, wet floors and work around pressure vessels and hot chemicals.
Are brewpubs a good place for chefs to start brewing?
Often. Brewpubs pair beer with food and value someone who understands both the kitchen and the brewhouse.
